message.content: In June 2020, a review was published by two authors in Clinical reviews in allergy & immunology regarding the relationship between hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS), Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS), and Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS). Using PubMed, go to the 2nd publication (published in 2008) that this review references, and identify the geneticist who published the classification of one of the previous syndromes in 1998. What is the title of this geneticist’s first publication in The Practitioner?

## Abstract

* * *

In recent years, an association between hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS), mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) has garnered attention and patients are increasingly presenting with this triad. However, a real relationship between these entities is unclear due to a lack of scientific validity. We conducted an extensive review of the literature using two different search strategies. A narrower strategy included 88 searches of various combinations of terms for each of the three conditions, yielding 19 unique papers. A broader search included 136 searches of various combinations of terms but included all forms of EDS and yielded 40 unique papers. Of these, only four and nine papers from the narrower and broader search strategies were original research articles. None of these papers resulted from a combination of the search terms for the three conditions. All three clinical entities are controversial in either existence or pathogenesis. MCAS is a poorly defined clinical entity, and many studies do not adhere to the proposed criteria when establishing the diagnosis. Patients previously diagnosed with EDS hypermobility type may not meet the new, stricter criteria for hEDS but may for a less severe hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD). The pathophysiology of POTS is still unclear. An evidence-based, common pathophysiologic mechanism between any of the two, much less all three conditions, has yet to be described. Our review of the literature shows that current evidence is lacking on the existence of MCAS or hEDS as separate or significant clinical entities. Studies proposing a relationship between the three clinical entities are either biased or based on outdated criteria. The reason behind the purported association of these entities stems from an overlapping pool of vague, subjective symptoms, which is inadequate evidence to conclude that any such relationship exists.

**Peter H. Beighton** [FRSSAf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_of_South_Africa "Royal Society of South Africa") (1934 – 14 June 2023) was a British-born South African medical [geneticist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneticist "Geneticist"). He is known for inventing the [Beighton Scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beighton_Scale?action=edit&redlink=1 "Beighton Scale (page does not exist)") for [joint hypermobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_hypermobility "Joint hypermobility").

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Peter_Beighton&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Beighton was born in [Bolton, Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolton,_Lancashire "Bolton, Lancashire"), England, on 28th June 1934.[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) He qualified in medicine in 1957 at St Mary's Hospital, [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London").[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3) After several internships, Beighton served as a Medical Officer in the Parachute Regiment and with the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") forces during the [Congo Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_Crisis "Congo Crisis"). In 1966 Beighton began training in [internal medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_medicine "Internal medicine") at [St Thomas' Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Thomas'_Hospital "St Thomas' Hospital") in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London")[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3) and held a Fulbright research fellowship in clinical genetics in 1968-69 with Dr. [Victor McKusick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_McKusick "Victor McKusick") at [Johns Hopkins Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_Hospital "Johns Hopkins Hospital") in [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore").[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Peter_Beighton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Beighton undertook clinical research in the [Sahara Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahara_Desert "Sahara Desert") and epidemiologic studies on [Easter Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Island "Easter Island"), [Tristan da Cunha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_da_Cunha "Tristan da Cunha") and in Southern Africa. In 1970, he moved to [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), joining the Division of Orthopaedic Surgery at the [University of the Witwatersrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand "University of the Witwatersrand") earning a PhD.[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3) In the course of this work, he developed the [Beighton Scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beighton_score "Beighton score").[[3]](#cite_note-:0-3) In 1972, Beighton was appointed Professor of Human Genetics at the [University of Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cape_Town "University of Cape Town")'s Faculty of Medicine. His research was largely on inherited disorders of the skeleton and connective tissues.

Beighton received several awards including the gold medal of the [British Orthopaedic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Orthopaedic_Association "British Orthopaedic Association"), the President's Medallion of the South African Orthopaedic Association, the Smith & Nephew literary award and the silver medal of the South African Medical Research Council. In 2002, he was the first recipient of the newly established [Order of Mapungubwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Mapungubwe "Order of Mapungubwe") - bronze, which was bestowed for lifetime achievement as a scientist, and for research into the inherited disorders of the skeleton.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Beighton was a Fellow of the Royal Colleges of Physicians of London and Edinburgh. Beighton was accorded Fellowships of the University of Cape Town, the British Society of Rheumatology, the Royal Geographical Society and the Royal Society, SA. In 1999, at the age of 65 years he obtained the degree of Master of Philosophy in History by external thesis at the University of Lancaster, UK. Professor Beighton retired with Emeritus status at the end of 1999, retaining his links with UCT, and collaborating with the University of the Western Cape Faculty of Dentistry. In 2014 at the age of 80 years he was still employed part-time in the UCT Faculty of Health Sciences as a Senior Scholar.

Sixteen of Professor Beighton's postgraduate students have been awarded Doctorates, and ten of these have achieved Professorial status. Professor Beighton was the author, co-author or editor of 20 monographs and editions, 34 chapters and more than >430 medical publications.

Peter Beighton and his wife Greta Beighton shared an interest in the history of medical genetics and published two unique volumes of brief biographies of people for whom genetic syndromes have been named.

## Personal life and death

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Peter_Beighton&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life and death")]

Peter and Greta participated in the sport of orienteering for many years, and they were South African champions in their respective age groups on several occasions. Greta died in Cape Town on 29 May 2017.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

Peter Beighton died in Cape Town on 14 June 2023.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Based on my research, I've traced the chain of references:

1. **The 2020 review** by Kucharik & Chang in *Clinical Reviews in Allergy & Immunology* (June 2020) references the **2008 publication** by Parapia & Jackson: "Ehlers-Danlos syndrome – a historical review" in *British Journal of Haematology*.

2. **The 2008 Parapia & Jackson review** references the **1998 classification** of Ehlers-Danlos syndromes: "Ehlers-Danlos syndromes: revised nosology, Villefranche, 1997" published in *American Journal of Medical Genetics* (1998), authored by **P.
